abstract: Huntington's disease is an inherited neurodegenerative disorder with no disease-modifying treatment available. Preclinical trials of gene therapies rely on large animal models and the transgenic Huntington's disease (TgHD) minipig is one of them. Minipigs live more than a decade, so the effect of a single dose of gene therapy can be followed for years. The TgHD transgene carries a mixed CAG/CAA repeat that is not expected to expand somatically. However, its putamen, part of the striatum that degenerates first in patients, had not been examined by genome-wide methods, nor beyond 4 years of age. We compared the putamen of transgenic and wild-type minipigs at 4 and 8 years by RNA sequencing and label-free mass spectrometry proteomics, and measured mutant huntingtin by immunoassay. Seven genes were differentially expressed at 4 years and 3,324 at 8 years, and the pathway changes of the transcriptome and the proteome were concordant at that age. The D2 medium spiny neuron marker gene set was reduced at 8 years in both the transcriptome and the proteome. Mitochondrial and oxidative phosphorylation pathways were positively enriched at 4 years and negatively enriched at 8 years. Immune and complement pathways were positively enriched at 8 years, and the number of altered splicing events increased almost fivefold between 4 and 8 years. We detected no age-dependent accumulation of soluble mutant huntingtin. Since the repeat does not expand, these changes developed without somatic expansion, a major driver of progression in human Huntington's disease. We propose that the reduced neuronal markers reflect a loss of neuronal identity rather than neuronal death. The TgHD minipig would then recapitulate the slow early phase of the disease, when treatment is arguably most likely to help.
